transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-10-02
- Start: 17:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Neill (Redwood SE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Valence CTO), Marco Silva (Valence ML Eng), Priya Desai (Valence Head of Platform), Tom Becker (Valence SRE)

Summary:
Quick migration kickoff for Valence Labs' plan to move production endpoints from a split vendor setup (OpenAI + Anthropic + TogetherAI for research) to a unified Redwood API + Private deployment for regulated inference. Goals: parity of response quality, predictable latency, cost targets, and SOC2-compliant auditability. Agreed next steps include pilot pricing, benchmark run, and technical deep dive for Private/VPC deployment.

Topics covered:
- Redwood API parity mapping and adapter patterns
- Console demo: routing, rollouts, and observability
- Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, quantization, KV/prefix caching
- Private deployment considerations: VPC, KMS/HSM, SSO, audit logs, network egress
- Pilot plan, timeline, and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give a fairly focused run today, hi Aisha, hi team. Quick intros then we'll jump into the parity mapping and the console so you can see where things plug in.
[00:18] Aisha (Valence CTO): Hi Maya, thanks. We're excited, we want to consolidate vendor surface area but keep the best quality for chat and code endpoints. Marco will walk you through traffic patterns after the demo.
[00:28] Liam (Redwood SE): Great. Real quick, we usually do AE context, SE demo. I'll show the runtime behaviors, batching and cache bits, and Diego will touch private deploy patterns.
[00:38] Marco (Valence): Sounds good. One note: we currently route 60% of production QPS to OpenAI for chat and 30% to Anthropic for longer summarization, 10% to Together for research-only models. Latency P95 targets are 750ms for chat, 2.5s for long summarization windows.
[00:58] Maya: Perfect, that'll guide the parity mapping. Ok Liam, take it away.

[02:10] Liam: Alright, I'll start with the API surface. Redwood's REST/SDK mirrors common calls — generation, chat, embeddings — and we keep model aliases so you can map openai:gpt-4 style names to a Redwood model. For parity, we do model variants and prompt templates. Example: you can pin a 'chat-stable' variant that tries to match OpenAI chat behavior and a 'summarize-long' variant tuned for Anthropic-like answers.
[02:40] Priya: How much work is the adapter layer? Do we need to rewrite a ton of code?
[02:46] Liam: Minimal. We provide a lightweight adapter shim — often a single line change to switch endpoints plus a small mapping for function-calling and any schema differences. Real world, most customers do config-driven routing and keep their prompts intact.
[03:08] Diego (Redwood SE): Also note we support function/tool calling and structured outputs; occasionally the tokenization differences cause slight length shifts but nothing that forces prompt rewrites in our experience.

[04:10] Aisha: For quality parity, we need to run A/Bs. Will Redwood help with rollouts?
[04:18] Maya: Yes, console rollouts are first-class: canary, percentage-based, rollback on latency/error spikes, and automatic fallback to a warm compatible variant. We'll show the console in a second.

[06:05] Liam: Moving to runtime optimizations — continuous batching cuts per-token cost but we tune it to keep P95 low. We also do automatic prefix/KV caching so repeated prefixes don't re-execute, that's huge for your 40% repeat queries.
[06:28] Tom (Valence SRE): Can you expand on KV cache — is it customer controlled, or is it managed?
[06:35] Liam: It's runtime-managed; policy is configurable. You can set TTLs and size limits, and export metrics. For Private deployments you can choose whether keys are stored in local SSD or remote cache. Some customers call it 'K-V cash' in logs which always amuses.

[08:00] Marco: About quantization — we saw mention of 4-bit quals in docs. How aggressive is that for preserving hallucination/quality?
[08:08] Diego: Good question. Our 'Optimize' toolkit recommends quantization profiles based on your workload. For chat endpoints we often use mixed precision or int8 + selective fp16 layers; for summarization we are more conservative. We'll include model-specific recommendations in the benchmark report.

[10:12] Priya: Compliance — SOC2, ISO, and KMS. We operate in a regulated vertical so audit logs and key control are mandatory.
[10:22] Maya: Understood. Our Private offering supports bringing your own KMS/HSM and the control plane can be set to a customer VPC. We provide detailed audit logs, SSO via SAML, role-based access, and paper SOC2 docs. We'll attach the security pack after the call.

[12:45] Aisha: For private, what's the approximate infra footprint you'd expect for our current throughput? Marco mentioned numbers but to restate: 1.2k qps peak, average 350qps, with 40% chat, 30% embeddings, rest long-ops.
[12:58] Liam: With Redwood Dedicated sizing guidance, that's roughly N GPU nodes — I'll avoid over-claiming on the call — but we'll run a cost/throughput model in the benchmark template. For pilot we'll suggest a scaled cluster to replicate your p95 latencies.

[15:30] Marco: About routing — can we do request-based routing by path and region? We want EU data to stay in EU and fall back to hosted for dev only.
[15:42] Diego: Yes. Smart routing policies can be per-route. Keys can be region-scoped and we support route-level model pins and fallbacks. You can also configure fallthrough to hosted or a cheaper variant during capacity spikes.

[18:20] Priya: Any gotchas moving function-calling from OpenAI? We use it heavily.
[18:29] Liam: The wire is similar; the schema for function calling is almost identical. The main work is ensuring your function signatures and error handling align. We can also translate a few edge cases during the pilot.

[20:00] Aisha: Can Redwood run our current fine-tuned/LoRA models? We have some tuned models on TogetherAI.
[20:08] Diego: We can host many open model formats; if Together's weights are exportable to standard checkpoints we can run them. Some model-specific kernels are needed. We can map to an equivalent open variant or run your fine-tuned artifact in Private. We'll need sample artifacts for the deep dive.

[22:40] Marco: Benchmarks — we want apples-to-apples. Do you run token-level pacing + request shaping in the same way?
[22:48] Liam: We bake in the same prompt, same hardware profile, and note differences in tokenization. We'll run three buckets: dev hosted baseline, Redwood hosted parity, and Redwood Private with the optimized runtime. We'll produce p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost-per-1M tokens.

[26:10] Maya: Quick console demo — (screen share noises) — top left you see per-route dashboards, cost breakdown by token, per-token latency waterfall, and trace links. Here's the rollout panel; you can create a canary, choose percent, tie in regressions to automatic rollback policies.
[27:05] Priya: That latency waterfall — does it break down serving vs networking vs kernel time?
[27:11] Diego: Yes, runtime shows kernel/compilation/warmup and network egress. For Private its agent reports local metrics.

[30:00] Marco: About observability retention — our audit team needs 12 months of request logs for certain endpoints.
[30:07] Maya: We offer add-on retention tiers. For Private you control storage; for hosted we have enterprise retention add-on. We'll include pricing.

[33:00] Aisha: Success criteria for pilot — what do you suggest?
[33:07] Liam: We recommend three KPIs: 1) Latency parity within 15% of current P95s for chat, 2) Quality parity measured via holdout prompts with human evals and BLEU/ROUGE-like metrics — we'll help run these, 3) Cost no more than X% over current spend in Hosted pilot, then optimize below over time.

[35:20] Priya: Timeline — We're targeting a pilot before EOY and production in Q1 2027. Is that realistic?
[35:29] Maya: Yes, pilot in October/November is normal. We'll start with benchmark this week and follow with a private deployment deep dive.

[37:45] Tom: Network egress and data residency — do you require logs to pass through Redwood control plane for hosted? We prefer none for EU data.
[37:53] Diego: For Private, control plane can be in your VPC so nothing leaves. For hosted, metadata might pass through our control plane, but we have region restrictions and contractual terms for EU data. We'll include specifics in the security pack.

[40:10] Marco: A fairly tactical question — will we need to rewrite our retry logic? We rely on 429s and exponential backoff now.
[40:18] Liam: Redwood surfaces 429s and rate limit headers similarly. The main change is richer headers for batching/queueing. We can provide a middleware lib to normalize responses.

[42:00] Aisha: Ok, let's capture the immediate next steps and owners.
[42:07] Maya: Sure — I'll send pricing, SOW for pilot, and the benchmark template by Tuesday 2026-10-05. Liam, can you take the private deploy checklist?
[42:17] Liam: Yep I'll get that and a proposed 90-min deep technical session scheduled.
[42:21] Marco: We'll share top 50 prompts and 7-day traffic by Friday 2026-10-09.

[44:00] Priya: Also please include a sample k8s manifest and the recommended GPU types; our infra team will want that.
[44:08] Diego: We'll include an example manifest, autoscaling guidance and a sizing sheet.

[47:30] Maya: Final recap: pilot pricing + bench from me, deep-dive scheduling from Liam, artifacts and prompts from Valence. Security pack attached after call. Any other blockers?
[47:45] Aisha: Nothing else from us. This looks promising.
[48:00] Liam: One more note — during pilot we often recommend traffic shadowing on a small percentage to collect quality signals with no user impact. Marco, would that be possible?
[48:10] Marco: Yes, we can route 1% for 48 hours.

[49:30] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with calendar invites.
[49:40] Aisha: Thanks Maya, thanks team.
